source.title: Trade-Based Money Laundering: Trends and Developments

summary: GOLDEN LABEL, hand-drafted against the PDF. Joint FATF and Egmont Group survey of trade-based money laundering trends since the 2006 study: the four common techniques (over- and under-invoicing, over- and under-shipment including phantom shipments, multiple invoicing, false description of goods), Black Market Peso Exchange and its offsetting variant, newer illicit cash integration methods (surrogate shopping networks, infiltration of legitimate supply chains that use no misrepresentation), third-party intermediaries settling invoices, shell and front companies, exploitation of open account trade and MVTS/hawala, and trade-based terrorist financing. Fifteen case studies from the US, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and Israel; the remainder is challenges, FIU analytics and public-private partnership practice.

typologies.label: Offsetting or compensation schemes between criminal groups

citations.quote: A variation of Black Market Peso Exchange is called offsetting or compensation , whereby OCGs or PMLs dispose of illicit cash by cooperating with OCGs or PMLs looking for cash.

These companies take receipt of criminal cash from other criminal networks, providing a veneer of legitimacy by invoicing for building maintenance services; the funds are then transferred to wholesalers in Asia.

typologies.label: Surrogate shopping (Daigou) networks for illicit cash integration

citations.quote: whereby OCGs or PMLs provide local currency (the proceeds of crime) to these surrogate shoppers, who pay for desirable goods that are transported to another jurisdiction and passed to the OCG or PML.

students were making multiple purchases of portable electronics, such as smart phones and tablets. Their credit card balances were subsequently settled via electronic funds from companies suspected of laundering the proceeds of drug trafficking.

typologies.label: Infiltration of legitimate supply chains without trade misrepresentation

citations.quote: an OCG or PML purchases a stake in a legitimate business, which may or may not be struggling financially, and continues using its supply chain as a method of integrating illicit cash into the financial system.
They do not use any of the common TBML techniques, instead they exploit these legitimate supply chains to move their criminal proceeds to different jurisdictions.

typologies.label: Exploitation of MVTS and hawala for trade settlement

citations.quote: conspirators involved in a false invoicing TBML scheme have used MVTS to facilitate payment for the goods, rather than attempt payment via a bank
a network of MVTS and hawala was used in order to arrange settlements for the trade of goods between importer s in Country A and exporter s in Country B.
the report defines TBTF as “disguising the movement of value through the use of trade transactions in an attempt to finance terrorism , whether from legitimate or illegitimate sources”.
In this way, the terrorist organisation was able to transfer cash from country C to country A through the legitimate trade system by using commodity as currency.
SBML schemes rely on exploiting the trade in services or other intangibles to disguise and justify the movement of illicit proceeds.

actors.name: Organised Criminal Groups
actors.role: Exploit trade supply chains to launder proceeds of drug trafficking, smuggling and tax evasion; own lower-value supply chains end to end

citations.quote: OCGs, PMLs and terrorist financiers will exploit any sector, commodity, or service where they perceive an opportunity.
Supply chains moving lower-value goods are most at risk to end-to end ownership by a criminal organisation or PML network.

actors.name: Professional Money Launderers
actors.role: Specialist launderers taking receipt of OCG proceeds and moving them via TBML for a fee; TBML is one of their most preferred methods

citations.quote: These PMLs take receipt of the criminal proceeds on behalf of the OCG and transfer or convert those proceeds, including via TBML schemes
In professional ML networks, ML activity, including TBML, is carried out by one group of criminals, while the predicate offences are committed by other criminals.

actors.name: Terrorist financing networks
actors.role: Penetrate existing trade chains and complicit MVTS to move value to terrorist organisations without direct payments

citations.quote: using complicit MVTS to inject funds intended for TF purpose into the trade transactions, while avoiding making direct payments to the terrorist organisation.

actors.name: Mexican and European transnational criminal organizations
actors.role: Drug trafficking organisations named as the TBML threat in the U.S. national risk assessment; increasingly rely on Asian PMLs as money brokers

citations.quote: Threats like Mexican and European transnational criminal organizations (TCOs) and their associated drug trafficking activity, employ TBML schemes because their sophistication makes it difficult for authorities to detect.

actors.name: Central and South American drug cartels
actors.role: Launder US drug proceeds through Black Market Peso Exchange using complicit money brokers, cash controllers and importers

citations.quote: Another traditional type of TBML is Black Market Peso Exchange, which Central and South American drug cartels have used to launder drug proceeds generated in the United States.

actors.name: Asian professional money launderers (money brokers)
actors.role: Money brokers in traditional TBML schemes on whom TCOs increasingly rely, per the 2020 U.S. National Illicit Finance Strategy

citations.quote: the 2020 National Illicit Finance Strategy noted that TCOs are relying more on Asian PMLs who ser ve as money brokers in traditional TBML schemes.

actors.name: Surrogate shopper networks
actors.role: Individuals or syndicated groups buying luxury and portable electronic goods on behalf of OCGs or PMLs with criminal cash, with at least some knowledge of whom they act for

citations.quote: Some shoppers may also make purchases on behalf of OCGs to distance them from the asset, suggesting the surrogate shopper has at least some knowledge that what they are doing is on behalf of an OCG.

One such example of this is known as Daigou (which literally means surrogate shopping) whereby individuals or syndicated groups of exporters outside Asian countries purchase mainly luxury goods for customers in those countries.

extraction_notes: Golden label. Printed folio runs two behind the PDF index; pages 1, 2 and 66 carry none. Over-/under-shipment (quantity misrepresentation short of phantom) is a FATF foundation technique the library lacks; cited under TBML004, not made emergent. Sanctions evasion, dual-use goods (fn 11) and FTZs are mentioned once and not labelled; TBML010/SAN006 deliberately absent. Front companies are TBML009/PAT007, not SAN004: ML framing, not sanctions. Offsetting kept separate from BMPE as the report names it as its own scheme with a case. SBML labelled emergent (family other) although the report says it is not TBML, because it gets its own sector list. Anonymised case parties (Peruvian, Colombian, Italian, Brazilian/Portuguese nationals) are not actors; the Box 2.6 Mafia link is too thin. Jurisdictions are case and risk locations only; Peru, Canada and Mexico are actor origins or enforcement bodies and are excluded. BA007 carries the cash-integration theme; BA008 (Box 2.8 only) not labelled.
